```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

`gflow` studies scalar fields on graphs: where a field rises or falls,
which vertices belong to a basin, and how changes in two fields align.
Start with a task, then use the catalog to find its detailed help.
The [example graphs and fields](example-graphs-and-fields.html) introduce
inspectable inputs. The [canonical workflow](basin_complex_workflow_vignette.html)
covers construction and refinement in more detail; the
[noisy-circle workflow](noisy_circle_core_workflow_vignette.html) adds noisy
observations, graph selection, and local association.

```{r opening-result, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Two peaks on a seven-vertex path. The height-3 plateau joins the higher peak at field height 1; the tree records that relationship. Reproduce the analysis below."}
if (knitr::is_html_output()) knitr::include_graphics("figures/basin-showcase.png")
```

## Choose a starting point

| Your task | Entry point | Result or prerequisite |
|---|---|---|
| Start a basin analysis | `create.basin.complex()` | A graph, edge lengths, and one finite field give a `basin_complex`. |
| Follow connected level sets | The constructor with `method = "superlevel_merge_tree"` | Exact graph merge tree; query with `get.basin.merge.tree()` and `cut()`. |
| Follow field-directed paths | The constructor with `method = "trajectory_flow"` | Terminal basins and a trajectory forest. |
| Inspect support and coverage | `get.basin.table()`, `get.basin.membership()`, `get.basin.assignment()` | Retained support, raw overlap, and optional single assignments are different quantities. |
| Reconstruct an archived analysis | `as.basin.complex()` | Requires the original graph and an available construction field. |
| Extend position along a path into its neighborhood | `compute.harmonic.extension()` | A connected vertex path and a graph give harmonic coordinates. |
| Compare local changes symmetrically | `lcor()` | Graph plus vectors or matrices of vertex fields. |
| Measure change in a response along a directing field | `lslope()` or `lslope.neighborhood()` | Directed edge ratios or neighborhood regression coefficients. |
| Summarize flow polarity and overlap | `gfcor()`, `gfassoc.*()` | Currently requires archived basin/membership structures; no public canonical adapter yet. |

## A complete first analysis

This seven-vertex path has a plateau at vertices 2--3 and a higher peak at
vertex 6. No graph-construction package call or hidden workspace object is
needed. Edge lengths are one distance unit; field values have arbitrary field
units. Unit vertex masses express equal support, independently of field height.

```{r first-analysis}
library(gflow)
adjacency <- list(2L, c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 4L), c(3L, 5L),
                  c(4L, 6L), c(5L, 7L), 6L)
edge_lengths <- lapply(adjacency, function(v) rep(1, length(v)))
field <- c(0, 3, 3, 1, 2, 4, 0)
bc <- create.basin.complex(
  adj.list = adjacency, edge.length.list = edge_lengths, field = field,
  method = "superlevel_merge_tree", direction = "max",
  vertex.mass = rep(1, length(field))
)
stopifnot(identical(bc$status, "ok"))
tab <- get.basin.table(bc)
knitr::kable(tab[, c("extremum.vertex", "birth.level", "death.level",
                     "persistence", "raw.support.size")],
             caption = "Peak births and lifetimes on the seven-vertex path.")
get.basin.membership(bc)
get.basin.assignment(bc)
tree <- get.basin.merge.tree(bc, required = TRUE)
cut(tree, height = 2)$components
```

```{r first-tree, fig.cap="Ascending merge tree labeled by peak vertex. The plateau peak is born at 3 and joins the older peak at level 1; the component root spans levels 4 to 0."}
plot(tree, direction = "max", type = "tree", label = "extremum.vertex",
     show.mass = FALSE, show.support = FALSE)
```

The constructor accepts exactly the five full method strings in the next
table. `"merge_tree"` is **not** an alias. Use `edge.length.list` and `field`;
`weight.list` and `f` are not constructor aliases. Other functions, including
`lcor()`, do use `weight.list`, so check the selected function's help.

## Inputs, directions, and method choices

For `n` vertices, `adj.list[[i]][j]` is the 1-based index of a neighbor of
vertex `i`; `edge.length.list[[i]][j]` is the length of that same edge.
Both lists have length `n`. Neighbors must be unique, in range, and different
from the source vertex. Every edge needs a reverse edge of equal length
(within `graph.params$edge.length.symmetry.tolerance`, an absolute tolerance).
Lengths must be finite and nonnegative. Prefer positive lengths for derivative
or inverse-length calculations. Use `integer(0)` and `numeric(0)` for an
isolated vertex, rather than `NULL`.

The canonical validator accepts disconnected graphs and records components.
Exact merge trees work component by component, including isolates. This does
not guarantee that every backend and refinement can cover every component;
inspect `status`, `diagnostics`, and uncovered membership for the chosen method.
Never add artificial edges solely to hide disconnectedness.

Coordinates describe observation locations or a drawing. They are not an
argument to the canonical constructor: adjacency and lengths define its
geometry. `field` supplies one finite numeric value per vertex in graph order.
It may be observed, known, or estimated elsewhere. `vertex.id` optionally
preserves unique external IDs; indexing remains internal and 1-based, with
external-ID companion columns in the returned tables.

`vertex.mass` is nonnegative empirical or quadrature support with positive
total. The constructor normalizes it to sum to one for mass summaries and
mass-threshold refinement; it does not infer uniform mass when omitted.
Unavailable mass summaries are `NA`. Full support mass counts each containing
basin, whereas `raw.allocated.mass` apportions mass using raw membership
weights. Overlapping full support masses need not sum to one.
`vertex.density` is a separate nonnegative field that changes trajectory edge
scores only in density-modulated flow. Neither input estimates the other, and
mass does not redefine the exact graph level-set hierarchy.

`direction = "max"` follows increasing field values and `"min"` decreasing
values; `"both"` computes both orientations. Older help sometimes calls the
support reached *downward from a maximum* a descending basin. Here direction
always names the extremum toward which the analysis is oriented.

| `method` | Basin definition and controls | Distinct output |
|---|---|---|
| `"trajectory_flow"` | `modulation = "CLOSEST"` contracts connected exact plateaus, then chooses an improving boundary edge by length, target vertex, and source vertex. Other modes are `"NONE"`, `"EDGELEN"`, `"DENSITY"`, `"DENSITY_EDGELEN"`; these do not use the exact-plateau contraction. | Trajectory forest, terminal supports, optional primary labels. |
| `"superlevel_merge_tree"` | Connected sets with `field >= height` for maxima, or `field <= height` for minima. Only `plateau.tolerance = 0` is supported. Equal births use the smaller representative vertex as elder. | Hierarchical supports, births, merge events, component roots, persistence. |
| `"geodesic_reachability"` | Monotone geodesic reachability from extrema, with `edge.length.quantile.thld` limiting edges. Its strict-extremum/plateau behavior differs from the exact level-set method. | Possibly overlapping and incomplete supports; optional stored trajectories in the backend record. |
| `"rtcb"` | Relaxed trajectory-constrained basins. Controls include candidate-region size `n.min`, cumulative monotonicity control `m.min`, tolerance controls `tau0`, `kappa`, and path limits `k.max`, `h.max`, `d.path.max`. Use the method's own parameter definitions. | Constrained-path supports and recorded backend parameters; no canonical trajectory forest or backend primary assignment. |
| `"overlap_cell_complex"` | Requires `direction = "both"`. Merges basin overlaps using `basin.merge.overlap.thld`; three `min.*.cell.size.thld` controls filter ascending/descending and same-direction cells. | Cell summary, intersections, cluster mappings, complex graph, and simplified field. |

RTCB means relaxed trajectory-constrained basins in the implemented backend.
It searches a distance-limited candidate region and allows bounded cumulative
movement against the desired direction. `n.min` limits the initial number of
settled candidate vertices, not the retained basin size. `m.min` determines the
loss-to-gain allowance; optional `q.min` takes precedence. `run.max` limits
consecutive adverse steps; `tau0` and `kappa` define a local tolerance schedule;
`k.max` caps retained search labels per vertex, `h.max` caps path hops, and
`d.path.max` caps path length. This is not a resampling or trajectory-voting
procedure, despite the older guide's “robust trajectory-consensus” wording.

For trajectory flow, `edge.length.quantile.thld = 1` keeps the full edge-length
range. Lower values interact with `long.edge.fallback` (`"allow_and_flag"`,
`"allow"`, or `"forbid"`). `store.trajectories` and
`max.trajectory.length` control recording. CLOSEST uses
`plateau.policy = "connected_exact"`; other modulations require `"none"`.
A terminal plateau has no strictly improving neighbor, and its representative
is its smallest vertex. Optional field perturbation uses `tie.breaking = TRUE`
and an explicit `tie.seed`; it changes the construction field while preserving
the caller's random state. Record that choice when comparing exact ties.

The shared schema is a navigation and provenance contract, not a claim that
these methods produce identical basins. Do not transfer parameters or infer
statistical robustness from a method's name. The overlap-cell backend also
requires compatible `dgraphs` graph operations; a recoverable backend error
returns `status = "failed"` with diagnostic text, rather than usable cells.

## Read results through accessors

Check construction status before interpreting empty tables. Invalid inputs
raise errors; a recoverable backend failure can instead return a failed object.

| Accessor | Public schema and interpretation |
|---|---|
| `get.basin.table(bc)` | One row per basin: identity, `type`, `method`, `retained`, extremum vertex/value, `birth.level`, `death.level`, `persistence`, `parent.basin.id`; raw, retained, and primary support vertex lists, sizes, and masses; `raw.allocated.mass`, assignment and retention status. Non-applicable measures are `NA`. |
| `get.basin.membership(bc)` | Raw many-to-many rows: `vertex`, `direction`, `basin.id`, `membership.weight`, `membership.status`, `source.stage`, `is.primary`, and `vertex.id`. This is construction membership, not the refined support table. |
| `get.basin.assignment(bc)` | One row per vertex and requested direction when available: `basin.id`, weight, status, policy, `root.vertex`, `next.vertex`, and external-ID companions. `NA` labels with `not_applicable` mean no policy/result, not necessarily uncovered vertices. |
| `get.basin.merge.tree(bc)` | `basin.merge.tree` for the exact level-set method, otherwise `NULL`. Its documented `merge.table` records losing/surviving basins, merge plateau/vertices, level, persistence, and event status. |
| `get.basin.trajectory.forest(bc)` | For trajectory flow: named `next.vertex` and `root.vertex` vectors by direction, trajectories, recording status, modulation, plateau and tie controls. Reachability/RTCB recording does not create this canonical forest. |
| `get.basin.cells(bc)` | For overlap-cell construction: `cell.summary` (`family`, `cell.id`, `n.vertices`, `vertices`), `cells`, `basin.intersections`, `complex.graph`, `cluster.assignments`, `cluster.mappings`, `simplified.field`. Other methods return `NULL`. |

Use `required = TRUE` on the three structure accessors to reject absent
structures. Use `summary(bc)` for direction-specific ranking and availability
information; the printed summary includes a bounded ranking and separate raw,
retained, and assigned vertex coverage. `as.data.frame(bc)` gives the basin table.
`plot(bc)` shows the input field against vertex index. Select
`view = "merge_tree"` for the exact hierarchy, or supply an `n` by 2
`coordinates` matrix to `view = "assignment"` or `view = "overlap"`.
Choose `direction` explicitly if both were constructed. Failed construction is
labeled in the input-field view and rejected by analytical views; partial
results warn. These plots do not modify the analysis. `basin()` and `basins()`
also dispatch on canonical objects, but the non-colliding `get.basin.*()`
accessors make the intended schema explicit.

A vertex can be in multiple supports. Equal-share membership weights encode
overlap; they are not posterior probabilities. To find raw uncovered vertices
in a direction, subtract its membership vertices from `seq_along(field)`.
For refined coverage use the union of the table's retained support vertex lists.
Do not infer coverage from assignment alone. The
`"largest_membership_then_extremum"` assignment policy resolves eligible
membership using the implementation's size/extremum ordering. It is available
for trajectory and reachability methods. Reachability defaults to `"none"`;
RTCB currently records `"none"` even if `"backend_primary"` was requested.
Overlap cells have no primary assignment. Exact trees use `"elder_at_merge"`.

For an ascending merge tree, a branch is born at a maximum and dies when its
component joins an older branch as the height decreases. Persistence is
`birth.level - death.level`. For descending trees the height increases from
minima and persistence is `death.level - birth.level`. Both are nonnegative
and in **field units**. Each disconnected component has a surviving root whose
death is its opposite field extreme; a constant component has zero lifetime.
This finite root convention is not an observed merger into another component.
Hierarchical support can include child support, whereas primary assignment
keeps branch labels. Neither is the same as an exact level-set cut:
`cut(tree, height, direction)` returns active components and their membership.
Persistence measures lifetime across field thresholds, not a p-value or an
automatic significance test. `as.dendrogram(tree, direction, component)` and
`plot(tree, ...)` are views of this hierarchy.

## Refine or convert a basin analysis

Use `simplify.params` in the constructor. The fixed order is relative-value
filtering, maxima/minima clustering, geometric filtering, support filtering,
then expansion. Filtering changes retained flags/support and clears affected
assignments; clustering unions retained supports and remaps assignments;
expansion adds vertices to retained supports. Raw membership rows, weights, and their mass allocation survive refinement;
`is.primary` is refreshed where a current assignment matches a raw row. It
cannot describe vertices added to retained support. Inspect current primary
labels with the assignment accessor.

Relative-value, clustering, and geometric stages apply to trajectory flow,
reachability, and RTCB. Support filtering also applies to exact trees.
Expansion applies only to reachability and RTCB; overlap cells have their own
construction controls and reject canonical refinement stages. Positive
`min.basin.mass` requires supplied mass. Resolved controls are in `parameters`;
`provenance$refinement.stages` records stages, before/after counts, and snapshots.
The [example vignette](example-graphs-and-fields.html#refine-retained-support)
shows why retained and raw supports must be read separately.

`as.basin.complex()` leaves a canonical input canonical. For archived
`gfc.flow`, `basins_of_attraction`, or `basin_cx`, it **reconstructs** a canonical
analysis from the supplied original adjacency/length lists and an available
field. It does not simply relabel an old object or promise identical results.
`gfc.flow` uses its stored `y`; `basin_cx` uses `original_y`;
`basins_of_attraction` uses stored `y` or requires explicit `field` and permits
`method = "geodesic_reachability"` or `"rtcb"`. Review method/refinement controls
instead of assuming all archived settings are inferred. Conversion provenance
records reconstruction and preserves the archived object.

## Extrema, trajectories, and harmonic coordinates

`detect.adaptive.extrema()` expands graph neighborhoods subject to
`max.radius` and `min.neighborhood.size` and returns `gflow_local_extrema`.
Equal field values stop the adaptive detector's strict comparison, and its
neighborhood count excludes the center. It can accept a smaller neighborhood
before a more extreme vertex farther away. It differs from the fixed-radius `dgraphs::detect.local.extrema()` and that
function's `local_extrema` class: that detector uses the full radius, permits
equal values, and includes the center in its neighborhood count. `vertices(result)` uses the shared
`dgraphs::vertices()` generic and dispatches on the object's class; for gflow
adaptive extrema, `include.center = TRUE` includes the center exactly once.
Neither detector should be substituted for exact plateau merge-tree births.

For individual directed paths, `construct.madag()` builds a **monotonic
ascent directed acyclic graph** (MADAG): vertices and edges reachable by
strictly increasing paths from a source. A directed acyclic graph has no
directed cycles. `madag.bottlenecks()` reports vertices shared by enough paths
to a chosen sink. Limit path enumeration for large graphs. A basin-intersection
graph from `construct.gflow.graph()` instead has a vertex for each archived
basin and edges for shared support; it is not the original directed flow graph.

`compute.harmonic.extension()` fixes arc-length positions on a supplied path
and solves for neighboring coordinates that average their neighbors. Its tube
radius counts hops or shortest-path distance, according to `tube.type`.
With `use.edge.weights = TRUE`, inverse edge lengths supply the averaging
weights. Inspect `n.iterations` and `final.max.change`; this operation extends
a path coordinate, not a statistical response model. `apply.harmonic.extension()`
and comparison helpers operate on their own local-subgraph records. Plotting
and file-saving defaults differ: disable visualization/saving when only
numerical results are needed.

## Local association and inference

`lcor()` compares the vectors of field differences from each vertex to its
neighbors using a normalized inner product. It is symmetric when fields and
their transformation controls are exchanged. `type = "derivative"` weights by
inverse squared edge length; `"unit"` uses equal weights; `"sign"` retains
direction agreement. `hop.radius > 1` uses vertices reachable within that many
hops and, for derivative weighting, shortest lengths within the hop limit.
This is local alignment of graph differences, not an ordinary Pearson
correlation of observations in a neighborhood.

| Inputs (rows are vertices) | `lcor()` result, without instrumentation | `lslope()` result |
|---|---|---|
| Vector and vector | Length-`n` coefficients | Length-`n` coefficients |
| Vector and matrix, or matrix and vector | `n` by number-of-columns matrix | Vector directing field plus response matrix is supported; matrix directing field plus vector is rejected. |
| Two different matrices | `n` by `ncol(y)` by `ncol(z)` array | All directed pairs in the same array shape |
| Identical matrices | `n` by number-of-unordered-pairs matrix, excluding diagonal | All directed pairs; no symmetric shortcut |

Numeric data frames are converted to matrices. `instrumented = TRUE` exposes
diagnostics where supported; use the documented result fields rather than
assuming that a plain matrix is a list. Keep `mc.cores = 1L` for portable
matrix-pair computations.

`lslope()` chooses an improving edge by the largest field difference in the
requested direction, then measures change in `z` relative to change in `y`.
This current edge selection is based on field differences, not their ratio to
edge length. At extrema without an improving edge the reported coefficient is
zero. `type = "slope"` has response-units per directing-field-unit;
`"normalized"` compresses the ratio, and `"sign"` keeps its sign information.
For ordinary signed continuous fields explicitly set both difference types to
`"difference"`: `lslope()` defaults to `"logratio"`. Log ratios require values
compatible with the positive pseudocount transformation.
`lslope.neighborhood()` accepts two vectors and uses all incident differences
in a weighted regression through the origin, returning coefficients, local
scales, and local correlation. None of these functions requires a fitted model.

```{r local-association}
response <- 2 * field + 1
data.frame(
  vertex = seq_along(field),
  alignment = as.numeric(lcor(adjacency, edge_lengths, field, response)),
  directed.slope = as.numeric(lslope(
    adjacency, edge_lengths, field, response,
    y.diff.type = "difference", z.diff.type = "difference"))
)
```

An association estimate, a permutation test, and a posterior summary answer
different questions:

* `permutation.test.lcor()` holds adjacency and edge lengths fixed and
  recomputes local correlations and a feature summary on every permutation.
  `permute = "z"` applies one common row permutation to all feature columns,
  preserving their within-row relationships; `"y"` permutes the response.
  It does not reconstruct graphs, refit fields, or reselect neighborhoods.
  Only its exposed difference/weighting controls are forwarded; there is no
  `hop.radius` argument in this test. Its statistics are `"mean.abs"`,
  `"max.abs"`, and the upper-tail signed `"mean"`. The Monte Carlo p-value is
  `(1 + number at least as large as observed) / (n.perm + 1)`.
* That test requires exchangeability of the permuted vertex rows under the
  null, conditional on the held-fixed inputs. Spatial dependence, repeated
  subjects, or a graph selected using the tested fields can invalidate
  unrestricted permutation. No block/stratum permutation control is exposed.
  `q.value` is the Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment across feature tests, not
  vertex-wise testing. False discovery rate control requires valid p-values
  and the procedure's independence or suitable positive-dependence conditions.
  Increasing permutation count improves resolution, not exchangeability.
* `lcor.with.posterior()` takes a fixed `y.hat` and supplied `n` by `B` field
  draws, or a list of such matrices for multiple features. All fields must be
  finite numeric values and all features must have the same positive draw
  count; inconsistent counts are rejected before computation. Supplied feature
  names are preserved, and supplied vertex names must agree in order (see
  `help("lcor.with.posterior", package = "gflow")`). It computes local
  correlation for each draw and returns feature-by-vertex means, standard
  deviations, and equal-tail quantile intervals. The graph and response remain
  fixed. It fits no posterior model and does not propagate uncertainty absent
  from those inputs. Intervals are pointwise, not simultaneous; their posterior
  interpretation depends on how the draws were obtained.

## Flow-aware association: current input boundary

`gfcor(y.hat, z.hat, y.basins, z.basins)` accepts two vertex vectors and two
archived `basins_of_attraction` objects. **It currently rejects canonical
`basin_complex` objects.** `gfassoc.membership()` has the same basin-class
restriction. The retired constructor must not be called to create these
inputs; use these interfaces only for compatible saved analyses. There is no
public conversion from canonical basins to that archived class.

`gfassoc.membership()` divides a vertex's membership equally among its
containing basins and forms maximum/minimum cell memberships. Its basin/cell
index arrays are **0-based positions**, unlike its 1-based extremum vertices.
`gfassoc.polarity()` combines these memberships with one field to locate each
vertex between accessible minima and maxima. `"value"` uses normalized height;
`"rank"` uses within-cell ranks. Invalid or flat ranges are marked, and should
not be read as zero association.

`gfcor()` aggregates products of the two polarity coordinates at vertex,
basin, and global levels. `A_pol` is mean polarity concordance and `kappa_pol`
summarizes sign concordance. Its `confidence` field is absolute association
magnitude, **not** a calibrated confidence probability. Unlike the canonical
constructor, `gfcor()` defaults to uniform aggregation weights if mass is absent.
`gfassoc.overlap()` sums products of soft memberships with optional vertex
mass. `gfassoc.deviation()` compares an overlap matrix with its row/column
marginal-product expectation and returns residuals; it does not perform a
permutation or chi-squared test. These summaries describe supplied structures;
association does not establish causation.

## Function catalog

The catalog covers 112 explicit exports: 111 locally defined functions and
one dependency re-export. There are also 99 S3 registrations, including three
names that are explicitly exported as well. Each explicit export appears exactly once below. **Start** means a recommended
entry point; **Advanced** means a working specialized interface with its own
input schema, not a claim of validation for every dataset; **Archive** means
an interface to older objects or their component records; **Retired** means
an exported function that raises a migration error. These labels distinguish
availability from recommendation. Open exact arguments with
`help("function.name", package = "gflow")`.

<!-- export-catalog-start -->

### Basin construction and conversion

| Function | Purpose | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `create.basin.complex()` | Construct a canonical basin analysis with a chosen method. | Start |
| `as.basin.complex()` | Validate a canonical object or reconstruct from a supported archive. | Start |
| `compute.basins.of.attraction()` | Retired reachability constructor; use canonical `geodesic_reachability`. | Retired |
| `compute.gfc()` | Retired composite refinement workflow; translate controls into canonical construction/refinement. | Retired |
| `compute.gfc.trajectory()` | Retired trajectory constructor; use canonical `trajectory_flow`. | Retired |
| `compute.gfc.flow()` | Retired trajectory alias; it also raises a migration error. | Retired |
| `create.basin.cx()` | Retired overlap constructor; use canonical `overlap_cell_complex`. | Retired |
| `compute.gfc.basins()` | Compute a specialized modulated-flow basin record (`gfc_basins`). | Advanced |
| `find.gflow.basins()` | Find path-based graph basins with size and edge controls. | Advanced |
| `create.gflow.cx()` | Construct an extrema-oriented complex with iterative harmonic modification. | Advanced |
| `create.morse.smale.complex()` | Construct a separate two-dimensional grid complex from `f.grid`. | Advanced |

| `get.basin.assignment()` | Read current optional single-basin labels and their status. | Start |
| `get.basin.merge.tree()` | Extract the exact level-set hierarchy. | Start |
| `get.basin.trajectory.forest()` | Extract canonical trajectory-flow paths and successor/root records. | Start |

“Spurious,” “probability,” and “persistence” in older function names do not
by themselves imply a calibrated statistical test. Prefer the exact canonical
tree for graph level-set births and mergers.

### Refinement and membership

| Function | Purpose | Status |

### Domain-specific visualization and supporting grid tools

The three extrema-labeling functions add labels/segments to an existing native
`rgl` scene and return invisibly; they do not return `ivue` widgets. Optional
`ivue` scene layers are a separate rendering workflow and are not needed for
these static examples. `draw.basin()` also adds to a native scene; its current
implementation looks up a free `graph.3d` object rather than accepting
coordinates explicitly, so it is not a self-contained new-analysis entry point.
Grid utilities here support the separate two-dimensional Morse--Smale workflow;
they are not a general synthetic-data API.

## Generic methods and object workflows

R's S3 dispatch selects a method from an object's class when a generic is
called. For canonical basins use `print()`, `summary()`, `plot()`,
`as.data.frame()`, `basin()`, and `basins()`. For exact trees use `plot()`,
`cut()`, and `as.dendrogram()`. Those last three method names are also explicit
exports and occur once each in the catalog, not twice.

Use `print()`/`summary()` on local-association, harmonic, adaptive-extrema, and
MADAG results as available. The remaining registrations below record historical
or specialized schemas; their presence does not make them canonical entry
points. In particular, names such as `basin.trajectories` are S3 registrations,
not independent constructors. Some historical generics (`list.cells`,
`cell.trajectories`, `lmax`, and others) are internal and should not be used as
new public workflows. Class names are shown here only to make dispatch and
coverage inspectable.

<!-- s3-catalog-start -->

## Migration and package boundaries

These instructions are available in installed help as
`help("gflow-migration", package = "gflow")`, as well as here.

| Earlier call or family | Current action |
|---|---|
| `detect.local.extrema()` in gflow | Use `gflow::detect.adaptive.extrema()` and recompute saved objects with the new class. The dgraphs detector has different semantics. |
| The five retired basin constructors | Use `create.basin.complex()` with the method and named parameter lists documented above; convert compatible archives with `as.basin.complex()`. No exact equivalence for every old argument combination is promised. |
| Generic graph construction, conversion, paths, and diagnostics | Use the documented public `dgraphs` API, with its current graph input/output schema. For example, `dgraphs::create.path.graph()` constructs a path; `dgraphs::detect.graph.endpoints()` handles endpoint diagnostics. |
| Generic graph layout | Use the appropriate layout package, for example optional `grip` for its documented layouts. A drawing is separate from the graph/field used for analysis. |
| Generic 3D rendering | Use `ivue::plot3D.plain()`, `ivue::plot3D.cont()`, `ivue::plot3D.groups()`, and scene layers such as `ivue::layer3D.path()` and `ivue::layer3D.edges()`. |
| Archived response smoothing / conditional-expectation estimators | `gflowx` is the archive for reproducing those analyses. Current `geosmooth` is a separate smoothing package, not an automatic drop-in replacement for every retired function. |
| Removed one-dimensional model-averaging functions (`magelo`, `mabilo`, `fit.pwlm*`, related families) | Extracted to `malo`; gflow no longer provides forwarders. Check that package's public help for the specific estimator. |
| PHATE, diffusion/potential pseudotime, quadratic-form geodesics, random-walk smoothing experiments | Removed from the gflow API. No supported successor is claimed here. |
| Removed generic weighted-p-value helpers and `fassoc*` tests | No public core adapter. Choose an inferential procedure for the actual estimand; flow-aware descriptive summaries are not replacement tests. |

Do not assume a renamed dependency function accepts the same object or
arguments. These package boundaries do not require installing sibling packages
to run the examples in this guide.
